clue.text: Prevent completion of work on street

parts.note: ST is the standard abbreviation for street
OP is short for opus, a musical work

explanation.surface: Roadworks on a street are blocked before they can be finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Completion of' tempts you to take a last letter, but it belongs to the definition. 'On' tells you the work comes after the street.
explanation.definitionFit: To halt something midway is to keep it from being finished, an ordinary verb sense.

clue.text: Drip fled naked after fool

parts.note: to trick someone is to fool them

indicators.note: something naked is stripped of its covering, so the word loses its outer letters

parts.note: the inner letters of this word, without its first and last

explanation.surface: A drip of a man ran off without his clothes after being made a fool of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the fool piece first. This puzzle has many clues on the theme of fools.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe liquid falling slowly in small drops, so they are close synonyms.

clue.text: Fool primarily expected to talk foolishly

parts.note: a prat is British slang for an idiot

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter is wanted

parts.note: the first letter of this word

explanation.surface: An idiot can be counted on, first and foremost, to babble nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: PRAT is everyday British slang for a stupid person.
explanation.definitionFit: To prate is to chatter at length about nothing much, idle empty talk.

clue.text: Second act precedes retreat

parts.note: a turn is a performer's act on stage
to second a proposal is to back it

explanation.surface: In a play, the second act comes before the characters withdraw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second act' reads as a single stage term, but the two words are separate pieces, and 'precedes' puts the act before the second.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn back is to give up going forward and head the other way, which is to withdraw.

clue.text: Seconds to stop fool revealing part of body

indicators.note: seconds here means the letters in second place of each following word

parts.note: the second letter of each of these three words

explanation.surface: Someone has seconds to stop an idiot from exposing his body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seconds' looks like a measure of time; it asks for the second letter of each of the next three words.
explanation.definitionFit: A digit on the foot is one of the small parts of the human body.

clue.text: Shake up loud vacuous fool stopping us here unexpectedly

indicators.note: to stop a gap is to plug it, so these letters sit inside the others
what happens unexpectedly breaks the usual order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: these six letters are rearranged
F is forte, the musical direction for loud

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so the word is emptied of its inside letters

parts.note: only the outside letters of this word

explanation.surface: A loud, empty-headed idiot suddenly halts our progress, causing a shake-up.
explanation.walkthrough: Three letters, F and FL, go inside the rearranged US HERE, near its end.
explanation.definitionFit: A reshuffle, as of a government cabinet, reorganises who does what, which is a shake-up.

clue.text: Fool recited great passage

indicators.note: something recited is spoken out loud, so we go by sound rather than spelling

parts.note: great is BIG and a passage between seats is an AISLE

explanation.surface: A fool stands up and declaims a great passage of verse.
explanation.walkthrough: Said quickly, BIG plus AISLE runs together into a close match for the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To beguile someone is to charm and deceive them, which is a way to fool them.

clue.text: Monarchy replacing Republican with Liberal fool

indicators.note: replacing means putting one thing in place of another, so one letter swaps out

parts.note: the Crown stands for the monarchy as an institution
R is the abbreviation for Republican
L is the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: A political joke: overthrowing the monarchy for a republic, then a liberal, only to end up with a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: The R in CROWN is swapped for L.
explanation.definitionFit: A clown is a comic performer, and by extension anyone who behaves like an idiot.

clue.text: Nastiest corrupt individual of immense strength

indicators.note: corrupt means spoiled or debased, so the original order of letters is broken

parts.note: these eight letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The most vicious crooked person also happens to be enormously powerful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nastiest corrupt' reads as a description of one villain; the adjective is the instruction to rearrange the superlative.
explanation.definitionFit: A titaness is a female Titan, one of the giant gods of Greek myth famed for great power.

clue.text: Develop good part of grid

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for good
a grid is made of rows and columns

explanation.surface: A useful section of the electricity network gets developed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of grid' looks like a hidden-word signal, but it is a definition of a row.
explanation.definitionFit: To grow is to increase in size or maturity, which is to develop.

clue.text: Offshore part of UK broadcaster close to collapse

parts.note: Sky is a British satellite television company

indicators.note: the close of something is its end, so only the final letter is taken

parts.note: the last letter of this word

explanation.surface: A British broadcaster's offshore arm is on the verge of going under.
explanation.walkthrough: 'UK broadcaster' looks like one phrase, but UK closes the definition and the broadcaster stands alone. Sky is a UK pay-TV network.
explanation.definitionFit: Skye is a large island off Scotland's west coast, so it lies offshore yet within Britain.

clue.text: Meetings concerning groups supporting workers

parts.note: re means about or concerning, as in a letter heading
trade unions are bodies that support workers

explanation.surface: Meetings about labour organisations that back employees.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one sentence about labour politics; it splits after the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Reunions are gatherings of people coming together again, a particular kind of meeting.

clue.text: Deny judge accepts one fool returning

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: to rate something is to judge its worth

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came, so these letters run backwards

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
to dupe someone is to fool them

explanation.surface: A judge takes in a fool on the way back and then denies it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Judge' looks like the person on the bench, but here it is a verb meaning to assess; the reversed fool and one sit inside it, just after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To repudiate a claim is to reject it as untrue or refuse to acknowledge it.

clue.text: Minor disturbance in this small vessel?

definitions.text: Minor disturbance in this small vessel?

parts.words: Minor disturbance in this small vessel?
parts.note: surface reading: a little rocking aboard a small boat

parts.words: Minor disturbance in this small vessel?
parts.note: setter's reading: the idiom 'a storm in a ...' means a fuss over nothing, and the vessel is a cup for a hot drink

explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' suggests a boat, but here it is a container for drinking from. A storm in a teacup is the British idiom for a fuss about trivia.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom places a petty commotion inside this little drinking cup, so the cup is where the minor upset happens.

clue.text: Fool cleaning woman with untrue story

parts.note: a char, or charwoman, is a British term for a cleaner
a falsehood is a lie

explanation.surface: A gullible fool of a cleaner comes out with a made-up tale.
explanation.walkthrough: A char is an old British word for a woman paid to clean houses.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a 'right charlie' is a silly person, an idiot who looks ridiculous.

clue.text: Wicked people right to be dropped by US sitcom

indicators.note: what is dropped is let go and left out, so a letter is removed

parts.note: Friends was a hugely popular American sitcom about six New Yorkers
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Villains insist the conservative actor be written out of an American comedy show.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the R from FRIENDS.
explanation.definitionFit: Fiends are demons or cruel evildoers, so they are wicked people in a strong sense.

clue.text: Abandon broadcast for fool?

indicators.note: a broadcast goes out over the air to be heard, so the sound matters, not spelling

parts.note: to abandon someone is to desert them

explanation.surface: Someone thinks about walking out on a fool and telling everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb to desert, stressed on the second syllable, sounds like the sweet course after dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: A fool is a cold pudding of puréed fruit folded into cream, served as a sweet course; the question mark flags the example.

clue.text: Sit astride bicycle seat holding traveller's coat

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it within, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: the seat of a bicycle is its saddle

indicators.note: a coat is the outer layer, so only the outside letters are taken

parts.note: the first and last letters of this word, ignoring the possessive

explanation.surface: A cyclist sits astride the saddle with a coat slung over it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coat' looks like a garment, but it signals the outer letters of 'traveller', which sit after the first letter of SADDLE.
explanation.definitionFit: To straddle something is to sit or stand with one leg on each side of it.

clue.text: Fool contributing to waste, as expected

indicators.note: something contributing to a whole is a part of it, so the letters lie inside the words

parts.note: the letters run across these three words

explanation.surface: An idiot adds to the rubbish pile, just as you'd predict.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run from the end of 'waste' through 'as' into the start of 'expected'.
explanation.definitionFit: To tease someone is to kid or have them on, which is to fool them playfully.

clue.text: Band like to enter in silence

indicators.note: to enter something is to go inside it, so one piece is placed within the other

parts.note: sh is the call for silence
as means like, as in 'white as snow'

explanation.surface: A music group would prefer to walk on stage quietly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Band' suggests musicians, but it means a strip of cloth. 'In' is part of the setting: the word for like sits within the call for quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: A sash is a long strip of fabric worn round the waist or over the shoulder, a band of cloth.

clue.text: Attack fool filling manuscript up

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means reading from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards
a filling sits inside something, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: MS is the abbreviation for manuscript
a sap is a gullible person

explanation.surface: A critic savages an idiot who has stuffed a document full of nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' only works as a reversal signal because this is a down entry, read from the bottom; 'Attack' here is a fit or seizure, not an assault.
explanation.definitionFit: An attack can mean a sudden bout of illness or feeling, as does a spasm of coughing.

clue.text: What was used during war to protect post?

definitions.text: What was used during war to protect
definitions.meaning: first meaning: chain armour worn by soldiers of old
second meaning: letters and parcels delivered by a postal service

explanation.surface: Something used in wartime to keep the letters safe.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one question about protecting the post in wartime; it splits into two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Chain armour of linked metal rings shielded medieval fighters, and the same word means letters delivered by a postal service.

clue.text: Strengthened new deal backing former monarch

parts.note: Queen Anne reigned over Britain in the early 1700s

indicators.note: something new is made afresh, so these letters are put into a fresh order

parts.note: these four letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A fresh agreement supporting a past ruler made her position stronger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New deal' sounds like Roosevelt's programme; the first word only asks for a rearrangement, which goes after the queen.
explanation.definitionFit: Annealing heats then slowly cools metal or glass to toughen it, so annealed material has been strengthened.

clue.text: Fool regularly forgetting anxiety

indicators.note: forgetting every other letter at a steady interval leaves only the alternate ones

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of this word; the reversed run inside 'forgetting' is a coincidence

explanation.surface: An idiot keeps forgetting to worry.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the first, third, fifth and seventh letters of 'anxiety'. Nit is short for nitwit.
explanation.definitionFit: Nit is British slang for a nitwit, a stupid person.

clue.text: What may accommodate men bound by principle?

indicators.note: to be bound by something is to be enclosed by it, so one piece sits inside

parts.note: a tenet is a principle or belief
taken as written

explanation.surface: A question about what will make room for people who are tied to their beliefs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Accommodate' doubles as housing in the definition and as holding in the surface; the question mark admits a building houses more than men.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenement is a large building divided into flats, so it is somewhere that houses residents.

clue.text: Team playing final stage of game

indicators.note: playing with something means toying with it, so these letters are moved around

parts.note: these four letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A side competing in the last part of a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' suggests team sport, but the game is chess.
explanation.definitionFit: Checkmate, often shortened, ends a chess match when the king cannot escape capture.
